title: Time as a circle
hook: many churches walk the life of Christ every year, with colors and seasons

segments.voice: Yesterday, in your own words, and your line: just talk. Did you say something out loud, in the car or on a walk? That closed twelve days of ways to pray. Now, twelve days on the circle of the year. Day one hundred nine.

Walk into the same church once a month for a year and watch the cloth on the altar. Late November, it turns purple, or in some churches deep blue. At Christmas, white and gold. Then back to green for a while. In spring, purple again, for weeks. At Easter, white, bursting with lilies. One Sunday in late spring, everything is suddenly red. Then green, for months and months, all through the summer and fall. Nobody announces it. It's just there, like leaves changing on a tree outside the window. Those colors are a clock. A calendar you can see from the back row. Today's word is the name of the whole circle.
screen: `PURPLE, WHITE, GREEN, RED.` → `NOBODY ANNOUNCES IT.` → `A CLOCK FROM THE BACK ROW.`

segments.voice: The liturgical year. Liturgy comes from the Greek leitourgia, the work of the people, public service. The liturgical year is the church's calendar, and it doesn't count money or school terms. It walks through the life of Jesus, every single year. It begins, in the Western churches, with Advent: four weeks of waiting in the dark before Christmas. Then Christmas itself, the birth. Then Epiphany, God shown to the world. Then Lent, forty days in the desert. Then Holy Week, the cross, and Easter, the empty tomb. Then Pentecost, the Spirit, fifty days later. And then the long green stretch the church calls ordinary time. Easter moves every year, because it follows the moon; Christmas stays put. The Orthodox year starts in a different place, on the first of September, and runs its own rhythm of feasts and fasts. The book of Ecclesiastes says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Here's the idea underneath. Most of us live time as a line: deadlines, birthdays, one year after another. The church year makes time a circle too. You come back to the same stories every year, and you're a different person each time you meet them. The birth sounds different the year you have a baby. The cross sounds different the year you lose someone. Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans keep the full year, as do many Methodists and Presbyterians; many Baptist, evangelical and Pentecostal churches mark mainly Christmas and Easter. For those who keep it, the circle makes the calendar itself holy.
screen: `LEITOURGIA: THE WORK OF THE PEOPLE.` · `A YEAR THROUGH THE LIFE OF JESUS.` · `A TIME TO EVERY PURPOSE.` · `TIME AS A LINE, AND A CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find yourself on the circle. Settle, and breathe. Picture the seasons going round: waiting, birth, light, desert, cross, empty tomb, fire, and then the long green ordinary. Don't worry about the calendar date right now. Ask which season your own life feels like this month. Waiting for something? In a desert? Somewhere ordinary and green? If you pray, you can bring that season to God as it is. If you don't, just name it, and sit with it. Later today, look up where the church calendar actually is. The bell holds the time.
Liturgical year. The church's calendar of seasons and colors, walking through the life of Christ every year. Today's word.
Your line: time can be holy. Today, look up the season and color of the church calendar right now, and notice one thing in your week that matches it. Day one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many Methodist and Presbyterian churches follow the liturgical year, changing colors, readings and prayers with each season; many other churches celebrate mainly Christmas and Easter.

myth: the church year starts on January 1
in the Western churches it starts with Advent, in late November or early December. the Orthodox year starts on September 1.
Easter's date moves, but Christmas stays put
Easter follows the moon. Christmas is fixed on December 25 (though some churches reckon it by the old calendar).
every church keeps the full liturgical year
many Baptist, evangelical and Pentecostal churches mark mainly Christmas and Easter.

fork.setup: it's the first Sunday of Advent, in late November. after church a friend says, happy new year! what does she mean?
fork.reveal: in the Western churches, the liturgical year begins on the first Sunday of Advent, and the circle starts again with waiting.

original.note: Greek: public service, the work of the people. the root of liturgy.

trapdoor: what you thought: liturgy means old ritual, the same every week.
what it means: a year that walks through the life of Jesus, with its own seasons and colors, so time itself becomes holy.

what a scholar hears: in ancient Athens a leitourgia was a public service a wealthy citizen paid for, like a festival chorus or a warship. the Greek Old Testament used the word for worship in the temple.

sources.quoted: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven

notes: Liturgical colors vary by church: Western churches commonly use violet (or blue in some Advent traditions), white/gold, red and green; Orthodox color customs differ. Stated as what one might see; confirm.
Orthodox church year (indiction) begins September 1: confirm.
Which churches keep the full year versus mainly Christmas and Easter is a generalization; confirm the lists are fair.
Athenian leitourgiai (choregia, trierarchy) and the Septuagint's use of leitourgia for temple service: standard background; confirm.

'Easter follows the moon': the date is the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox (by the churches' reckoning). Christmas on 25 December; some Orthodox churches keep it on 7 January (Julian 25 December), noted in the myth reveal.
